findings.title: Kick and bass share a fundamental
findings.detail: Separated, the kick inside the drum stem lands on 53.9 Hz and the bass stem's fundamental is 55.2 Hz — 0.4 semitones apart, against the 3 semitones two low-frequency sources need before the ear reads them as separate pitches — and the kick sits 1.7 dB over the bass over its own hit windows. Their 25-250 Hz distributions overlap at -2.4 dB against a -4.0 dB ceiling for Trap. These are two measured objects, not one waveform split by an onset gate: the kick and the bass were separated before either was measured. Across 40 detected hits the sub moves -0.6 dB when the kick lands, so there is no sidechain getting the bass out of the way. Every kick re-triggers the note the bass is already holding, so the low end reads as one thick sound instead of a hit and a pitch. Worst at 0:00.6, across 6 flagged spans.

engineer.verdict: Phase, width and clarity are genuinely fine here — correlation 0.92, S/M 0.20, clarity 0.53 — so nothing structural is broken in the imaging. What's wrong is that the spectrum is upside down: spectral centroid sits at 141 Hz, tilt is -13.8 dB/decade against -4.7, 250-500 Hz is +22.1 dB over the Trap curve while 1-2 kHz is 12.9 dB under and air is 30 dB under. That's your muddy low end and your buried vocal in one measurement, and the master is clipping flat 167 times on top of it. Stop the clipping, then take the low-mid out of the sources — do not touch a fader on the vocal until you have.
engineer.the_one_thing: Pull 250-500 Hz out of the 808 and keys buses — it measures +22.1 dB against target and 34.7 dB above 1-3 kHz where Trap wants about 9.9 dB — and lift 1.6 kHz on the vocal instead of raising it; that one exchange fixes the small-speaker mud and the buried vocal together.
strengths: Mono-solid: correlation 0.92 against a 0.45 floor, mono sum costs only -0.17 dB, and the low end is dead centre at a 1.00 mono ratio — this will survive a club sub and a phone.
Width is right for the genre without tricks: side/mid 0.20 inside the 0.18-0.45 window, L/R matched to +0.01 dB.
Dynamics survived the loudness push: 5.9 dB crest and 5.5 dB micro-dynamics both inside the Trap windows, PSR 4.9/5.0 in range.
Elements stay separable — clarity 0.53 against a 0.45 floor, masking 0.44 under the 0.55 ceiling — so this is a tonal problem, not an arrangement problem.

prescriptions.headline: The master is clipping flat, 167 times
prescriptions.diagnosis: 1,233 samples are pinned at the ceiling in 167 flat-topped runs, the longest 27 samples — that's a plateau over half a millisecond wide, not a stray inter-sample peak, and inter-sample overs read 0, so this was printed into the file rather than created by conversion. The clipped frames carry 0.166 on the distortion index measured against this track's own clean frames, which means the squared tops are manufacturing high-frequency grit that is feeding straight into the 2-5 kHz harshness reading. The long run spans 0:04.1-0:19.1, i.e. most of the beat, and with low bass sitting +17.6 dB over target it is the 808 pushing the master into the wall.
prescriptions.root_cause: The 808 bus is running hot enough that its peaks are flattened at the master ceiling instead of being controlled before they get there.

moves.action: Trim the 808 bus down 4 dB and high-pass it at 28 Hz, 12 dB/oct, before anything hits the master.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ with the utility gain)
moves.why: Takes the source of the flat tops out of the ceiling instead of asking the limiter to catch it.

moves.action: Set the limiter ceiling to -1.0 dBTP with true-peak detection and 4x oversampling on, and pull its input 1 dB.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-L 2 — nothing on your list limits, so this one is outside it (stock: Ableton Limiter / Logic Adaptive Limiter with true-peak lookahead enabled)
moves.why: Gives back the 0.97 dB of headroom every platform asks for and stops the ceiling from being a clipper.

moves.action: Re-render and confirm zero flat-topped runs and a sample peak below -1.0 dBFS before doing anything else.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-L 2 metering (stock: Ableton Limiter GR meter plus a waveform zoom at 0:04.1 and 0:18.6)
moves.why: Confirms the squared tops are gone rather than just quieter.

prescriptions.alternative: If the stereo bounce is genuinely all you have, iZotope RX De-clip will round the tops back into shape, but it reconstructs a guess — it cannot return what the 27-sample plateaus removed.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't just lower the limiter ceiling and re-export — if the clipping happened upstream of it the flat tops are already printed, and turning the master down simply carries the distortion with it at a lower level.
prescriptions.done_when: The new render reports 0 flat-topped runs and true peak at or under -1.0 dBTP.

prescriptions.headline: Limiter pumps with the kick at 2 Hz
prescriptions.diagnosis: PSR is actually fine — 4.9 dB at the 10th percentile and 4.98 median, both inside Trap's 4-9 dB window — so the mix isn't crushed flat. The problem is that with only 2.7 dB of estimated gain reduction it is still producing a 0.166 distortion index and 167 ceiling-pinned runs, which means it is doing very little work but doing it violently. Pumping index reads 0.49 at 2.00 Hz, which is exactly the quarter note at 119.7 BPM: the detector is following the kick and 808, so the whole top of the mix breathes on every beat.
prescriptions.root_cause: The limiter's detector is being driven by the 60-120 Hz energy that already sits 17.6 dB over target, so the low end is modulating the entire spectrum.

moves.action: High-pass the limiter's detector at 90 Hz, set release to 150 ms, and back the input off until gain reduction peaks at 2 dB.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-L 2 (outside your list — no limiter in it) (stock: Ableton Glue Compressor into Ableton Limiter, with the Glue's sidechain EQ high-passed at 90 H…
moves.why: Stops the 808 from dictating when the hats and vocal get turned down.

moves.action: Put Decapitator before the bus fader, Style N, drive low, blended in — soften the 808's peaks with harmonics instead of letting the master limiter square them.
moves.tool: Soundtoys Decapitator (stock: Ableton Saturator, Soft Sine curve, Drive 6 dB, Dry/Wet 40%)
moves.why: Rounds the 808's peaks and adds upper harmonics, which both lowers what the limiter sees and gives the glide pitch definition on small speakers.

prescriptions.alternative: If you'd rather not saturate the 808, a slow bus compressor on the 808 (4:1, 10 ms attack, 100 ms release, 2 dB GR) does the peak-control half of the job without the harmonics.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't reach for a slower attack or a soft-clipper on the master to hide this — the modulation is coming from the low end feeding the detector, and hiding it just moves the distortion around.
prescriptions.done_when: The top end stops breathing on every quarter note, gain reduction peaks at 2 dB or less, and the distortion index drops back under 0.16.

prescriptions.headline: 250-500 Hz wall is what's burying the vocal
prescriptions.diagnosis: 250-500 Hz measures +22.1 dB against the Trap curve, 150-400 Hz sits 34.7 dB above 1-3 kHz where this genre wants about 9.9 dB, and boxiness at 300-600 Hz reads 15.5 dB. That is the small-speaker mud you're describing — a phone speaker reproduces almost none of your sub, so all it gives back is the 300 Hz shelf. It is also why the vocal feels buried: the detector found no sustained lead vocal at all, intelligibility reads 0.15, mid and presence are named as the masking bands, and 1-2 kHz — where a rap vocal's intelligibility lives — is 12.9 dB under target. You don't have a vocal level problem, you have a hole at 1-2 kHz with a mountain on both sides of it.
prescriptions.root_cause: The 808's harmonics and the keys/pad are both dumping energy into 250-500 Hz, with narrow resonances at 259, 318 and 924 Hz riding on top of it, and nothing in the arrangement is carrying 1-2 kHz.

moves.action: Notch the two measured resonances: -8 dB at 318 Hz with Q 8 and -6 dB at 259 Hz with Q 6.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: Kills the two peaks that measured 10.3 dB and 8.5 dB proud without touching the 808's weight.

moves.action: High-pass at 180 Hz, 12 dB/oct, and take a broad -4 dB at 400 Hz with Q 1.0.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: The keys are only carrying atmosphere down there, so the region can leave without anyone hearing it go — unlike the 808, which is the hook.

moves.action: High-pass at 100 Hz, notch -6 dB at 924 Hz Q 8, and lift +3.5 dB at 1.6 kHz with Q 1.2.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: Puts the vocal into the 1-2 kHz gap the mix has left open instead of fighting the 300 Hz wall with a fader.

moves.action: CLA-2A after the EQ, 3-4 dB of gain reduction on the loudest lines, to hold the 2.1 dB of level inconsistency in place.
moves.tool: Waves CLA-2A (stock: Ableton Compressor, 3:1, 10 ms attack, 100 ms release, 3 dB GR)
moves.why: Stops the quieter syllables falling back behind the beat once the masking is gone.

prescriptions.alternative: If the stereo file is all you have, the 318 Hz Q 8 and 259 Hz Q 6 notches are surgical enough to do on the master — but leave the broad 400 Hz cut off there, or the drums lose their body along with the pad.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't cut 300 Hz on every channel — spread the same cut across the 808, keys and drums and you'll end up with a mix that has no weight anywhere; take it out of the two elements the resonances were measured on.
prescriptions.done_when: The 150-400 vs 60-120 Hz ratio falls back inside the -17.0 to -7.5 dB window, 150-400 vs 1-3 kHz drops toward 9.9 dB, and the vocal sits through the whole beat without you touching the fader.

prescriptions.headline: 60-250 Hz is 13-18 dB over the Trap curve
prescriptions.diagnosis: Low bass 60-120 Hz reads 25.6 dB against an 8.1 dB target — 17.6 dB over, four times the ±3.5 dB this genre allows — and upper bass 120-250 is 13.4 dB over its own. What's interesting is that the sub itself is fine: 20-60 Hz energy measures -5.1 dB inside the -16.0 to -4.0 window. So this is not too much sub, it's too much of the 808's body and the kick's shoulder, and upper bass is the single most congested band in the mix at 0.75.
prescriptions.root_cause: The kick's body and the 808's second octave are stacked on top of each other in 60-250 Hz, which is also what's pushing the master into the ceiling.

moves.action: High-pass at 40 Hz and take -4 dB at 100 Hz with Q 1.2 so the kick stops doubling the 808's body.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: Kick definition already measures 9.3 dB, so the transient survives losing the body the 808 is already providing.

moves.action: Take -5 dB at 180 Hz with Q 1.0 and -3 dB at 90 Hz with Q 1.4, leaving everything below 60 Hz alone.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: Drains the most congested band while protecting the sub energy that's already sitting correctly in range.

moves.action: Check the balance on a phone speaker at 0:08 and again on headphones before you commit.
moves.tool: Soundtoys Decapitator bypassed — just A/B the render (stock: Any mono phone bounce)

settings.Check A: phone speaker, 808 should read as a pitch

moves.why: Confirms you removed congestion rather than the low end itself.

prescriptions.alternative: If you'd rather not carve the 808, pull the whole 808 bus down 4-5 dB and lift the drums and hats to match — the tilt problem is relative, and the top-end work in the air prescription does half of this on its own.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't high-pass the 808 at 80 Hz to clean this up — sub 20-60 Hz already measures in range and the glide is the record; the excess is in 90-250 Hz, not below it.
prescriptions.done_when: Re-analysis puts 60-120 Hz within ±3.5 dB of its 8.1 dB target, upper bass stops reading as the worst congested band, and the 808 reads as a note rather than a thud on a laptop speaker.

prescriptions.headline: Not bright — two narrow spikes at 3.2k and 5.5k
prescriptions.diagnosis: The harshness index reads 0.999 against a 0.36 ceiling, but psychoacoustic sharpness is only 0.95 acum against a 2.60 limit and sibilance is 0.26 against a 0.40 ceiling — so this mix is not bright, it is spiky. Two narrow resonances do all of it: 5539 Hz at Q 10.3 standing 20.0 dB proud, and 3200 Hz at Q 9.5 standing 16.7 dB proud, on a presence band already +6.6 dB while 1-2 kHz is 12.9 dB under. The 5539 Hz peak fires at 0:02.6, 0:08.8, 0:12.6 and 0:18.8 — that's a repeating element, almost certainly the hat/perc layer, and the squared clipped peaks are adding to it.
prescriptions.root_cause: A resonant hat or perc layer and a lead sound are each parking a high-Q peak in the presence band, and there's nothing at 1-2 kHz to give the ear anything else to hold on to.

moves.action: Dynamic bell at 5539 Hz, Q 10, up to -10 dB, threshold set so it only pulls on the loud hits.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (Dynamic EQ mode) (stock: Logic Channel EQ static bell at 5539 Hz, Q 10, -8 dB / Ableton EQ Eight narrow bell)
moves.why: Removes the 20 dB spike only when it fires, so the hats keep their shape on the quieter hits.

moves.action: Dynamic bell at 3200 Hz, Q 8, up to -7 dB.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (Dynamic EQ mode) (stock: Ableton EQ Eight narrow bell at 3200 Hz, Q 8, -6 dB)
moves.why: Takes the edge off the element that measured 16.7 dB proud at those exact timestamps without dulling the whole presence region.

prescriptions.alternative: If you can find which sample is ringing, replace it — a hat with a Q 10 resonance 20 dB above its neighbours is a bad sample, and swapping it beats notching it on every render.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't drop a wide presence cut or a de-esser across the master to fix this — sibilance already measures 0.26 against a 0.40 ceiling, and a broad cut will push 1-2 kHz, already 12.9 dB under, even further out of reach.
prescriptions.done_when: The worst 2-5 kHz resonance drops from 16.7 dB to under 3 dB and the harshness index falls under 0.36, with the hats still clearly audible at 0:08.8.

prescriptions.headline: Air is 30 dB under: check for a low-pass
prescriptions.diagnosis: 10-20 kHz measures -34.8 dB against a -4.8 dB target — 30 dB under, with brilliance at -7.4 and overall tilt -13.8 dB/decade against -4.7. That is not a taste decision, that is something filtering the top or hat samples that are band-limited. And what little sits up there is not useful: air-band correlation is 0.08 with 0.92 width and -2.67 dB of mono-sum loss, meaning it's decorrelated reverb tail, not hats. In Trap the hats are supposed to carry the top of the record and right now they don't reach past the brilliance band.
prescriptions.root_cause: Either a low-pass somewhere on the chain or band-limited hat/perc samples, leaving the top octave to reverb tails.

moves.action: Walk the chain and find the low-pass — check Decapitator's tone control and VintageVerb's high-cut/damping first.
moves.tool: Soundtoys Decapitator / Valhalla VintageVerb (stock: Any spectrum analyser on each bus solo, looking for a slope above 10 kHz)
moves.why: You can't boost air that a filter is removing downstream.

moves.action: Decapitator, Style E, low drive, blended in to generate harmonics above 10 kHz that a shelf can't create.
moves.tool: Soundtoys Decapitator (stock: Ableton Saturator, Drive 6 dB, Dry/Wet 50%, with the output high-shelved)
moves.why: Makes new top-octave content out of the hats themselves, which is the only honest way to fill a band that's 30 dB empty.

moves.action: High shelf +5 dB at 10 kHz, Q 0.7, in Mid-only (M/S) mode after the saturation.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Logic Channel EQ high shelf on a mono-summed duplicate / Ableton EQ Eight in Mid mode)
moves.why: Lifts the harmonics you just created without raising the 0.08-correlation side content that would smear the top.

prescriptions.alternative: Swap the hat samples for ones that actually have content above 10 kHz — if they're 128 kbps rips, no amount of shelving will build the band back.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't fix this with a big high shelf on the master — at -34.8 dB there's nothing up there to lift except the decorrelated tail sitting at 0.08 correlation, and you'll get hiss and phasiness instead of hats.
prescriptions.done_when: The air band lands within 4 dB of its -4.8 dB target, tilt moves toward -4.7 dB/decade, and the hats read as ticks rather than as a wash on headphones.

prescriptions.headline: Kick and 808 share a note with no ducking
prescriptions.diagnosis: The kick fundamental is 55.3 Hz and the bass is 54.9 Hz — 0.1 semitones apart — and their 25-250 Hz distributions overlap at -2.4 dB against a -4.0 dB ceiling. No sidechain was detected: the sub only moves -0.6 dB when the kick lands, so across 40 hits they sum at full level every time, and the collision markers land at 0:00.6, 0:02.1, 0:04.6, 0:08.1, 0:10.6, 0:12.1, 0:14.6 and 0:18.1. Kick definition itself is fine at 9.3 dB, so you're not losing the transient — the sustains are stacking, and that stack is a large part of why 60-120 Hz reads 17.6 dB over target and why the master clips.
prescriptions.root_cause: The 808 holds through the kick with no ducking, and both are sitting on the same fundamental.

moves.action: Sidechain the 808 to the kick: 4:1, 1 ms attack, 120 ms release, 4 dB of duck.
moves.tool: Nothing on your list does external sidechain — the CLA-2A has no key input — so use the stock compressor (stock: Ableton Compressor with the kick as external s…
moves.why: Opens a window for the kick transient so the two stop summing into the ceiling on all 40 hits.

moves.action: Bell -3 dB at 55 Hz, Q 2, so the 808 owns the fundamental and the kick owns the click.
moves.tool: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 (stock: Ableton EQ Eight / Logic Channel EQ)
moves.why: Separates the two by role rather than by pitch, since they're only 0.1 semitones apart.

prescriptions.alternative: If you want the 808 completely untouched, volume-automate a 40 ms dip on the 808 at each of the eight collision timestamps instead of compressing — more work, zero pumping.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't retune the 808 away from the kick or high-pass it at 80 Hz — the glide is the hook and this genre needs its pitch; duck the sustain instead.
prescriptions.done_when: The sub drops around 4 dB at each kick instead of -0.6 dB, the overlap reads at or under -4.0 dB, and the kick punches without the 808 audibly disappearing.

prescriptions.headline: Hits don't land: punch 0.33 vs a 0.45 floor
prescriptions.diagnosis: Across 107 onsets each hit averages only 4.5 dB above its own level 50 ms later, with a smearing index of 0.58 and low mid the weakest band at 0.25. The attack time itself is fine at 14.6 ms, so the transients exist — they're just sitting on a sustained low-mid wall that never gets out of their way, and the limiter is modulating on top of it. Do this one last: most of the punch comes back for free once 250-500 Hz drops and the limiter stops pumping.
prescriptions.root_cause: Sustained 250-500 Hz energy and a beat-synchronous limiter are filling the 50 ms after every hit, so nothing reads as an attack.

moves.action: After the EQ work is done, re-listen — then add a transient shaper with +3 dB attack and -2 sustain only if the hits still sit flat.
moves.tool: SPL Transient Designer — reaching outside your list, nothing you own shapes envelopes (stock: Ableton Drum Buss transients control / Logic's Phat FX Transient…
moves.why: Restores the attack-to-sustain difference without adding level the limiter would just take back.

moves.action: Shorten the 808 decay in the sampler so it stops filling the gap between hits, or trim the tail 15% at 119.7 BPM.
moves.tool: Your sampler's amp envelope (stock: Ableton Simpler decay / Logic Sampler amp envelope)
moves.why: Clears the 50 ms window after each onset that the punch measurement is looking at.

prescriptions.alternative: Instead of a shaper, parallel-compress the drum bus hard (10:1, 30 ms attack, 100 ms release) and blend it under — attack survives, sustain rises less.
prescriptions.do_not: Don't reach for the transient shaper first — right now the punch score is being dragged down by the low-mid wall, and shaping before you EQ means you'll shape twice and overdo it.
prescriptions.done_when: Punch index clears 0.45 and the clap reads clearly on a phone at low volume without you raising it.

session_plan: Fix the clipping first: trim the 808 bus 4 dB, high-pass at 28 Hz, set the master ceiling to -1.0 dBTP with true peak on, and re-render to confirm zero flat runs — nothing measured below this is trustworthy until it's gone.
Set the limiter's detector high-pass to 90 Hz and release to 150 ms, and put Decapitator on the 808 bus so the limiter stops pumping in time with the kick.
Do the main tonal work: notch 318 and 259 Hz on the 808, high-pass the keys at 180 Hz with a -4 dB dip at 400, then lift 1.6 kHz on the vocal and hold it with the CLA-2A.
Rebalance the bottom: -4 dB at 100 Hz on the kick, -5 dB at 180 and -3 dB at 90 on the 808, then sidechain the 808 to the kick for 4 dB of duck.
Deal with the top: dynamic notches at 5539 Hz and 3200 Hz, hunt down the low-pass, then Decapitator plus a Mid-only 10 kHz shelf on the hats.
Re-listen on a phone and only then decide whether the drum bus still needs a transient shaper — and re-render at -1.0 dBTP with no added limiting.
Pull the master output 1 dB before bouncing: clean gain analysis says -6.01 LUFS is reachable with no limiting at all, which is inside the Trap window.
engineer.mastering_verdict: Not ready. Three things block it independently: 167 flat-topped runs printed into the file, a true peak of -0.03 dBTP where every platform wants -1.0, and a spectrum that is 22.1 dB hot at 250-500 Hz and 30.0 dB light at 10-20 kHz — no mastering engineer can fix that balance without wrecking something else. Get the low-mid and the air sorted at the source, deliver at -1.0 dBTP with the limiter barely working, and note that at -5.04 LUFS you're already handing back 9.0 LU to Spotify for nothing.
